oggetti/luna/cosa: The Earth's only natural satellite, about 384,000 km away from us. It doesn't shine with its own light: it reflects the Sun's.
oggetti/luna/quando: Almost every night, but its appearance changes from day to day (the phases). The best time to observe it is between first quarter and full Moon.
oggetti/luna/dove: It moves along the same band of sky as the Sun and the planets. It rises in the East and sets in the West, about 50 minutes later each day.
oggetti/luna/come: With the naked eye you can see the dark "seas". With binoculars the craters appear, especially along the line between light and shadow (the terminator).
oggetti/luna/origine: From the Latin "luna", from the same root as "lux" (light): "the bright one".
oggetti/luna/storia: On 20 July 1969 the Apollo 11 mission took the first people to the Moon. The names of the seas (Sea of Tranquillity, Sea of Serenity) were given in 1651 by the Jesuit Giovanni Battista Riccioli.
oggetti/mercurio/cosa: The planet closest to the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System.
oggetti/mercurio/quando: Tricky: it can only be seen for a few days a year, low on the horizon, shortly after sunset or shortly before dawn.
oggetti/mercurio/dove: Very low in the West after sunset, or in the East before dawn. You need a clear horizon.
oggetti/mercurio/come: To the naked eye it looks like a pinkish dot in the glow of twilight. Never look for it with binoculars before the Sun has set.
oggetti/mercurio/origine: From the Roman god Mercury, messenger of the gods: the fastest planet on its trip around the Sun (88 days).
oggetti/mercurio/storia: It's said that Copernicus never managed to see it. The MESSENGER probe mapped it from 2011 to 2015.
oggetti/venere/cosa: The planet most like the Earth in size, wrapped in thick clouds that reflect a lot of light. After the Sun and the Moon it's the brightest object in the sky.
oggetti/venere/quando: For some months it can be seen in the evening after sunset, for other months in the morning before dawn.
oggetti/venere/dove: In the West after sunset (the "evening star") or in the East before dawn (the "morning star").
oggetti/venere/come: To the naked eye it's a brilliant white point that doesn't twinkle. With a small telescope you can see its phases, like the Moon's.
oggetti/venere/origine: From the Roman goddess Venus, goddess of beauty, for its splendour. The Romans called it Lucifer ("light-bearer") in the morning and Vesper in the evening.
oggetti/venere/storia: In 1610 Galileo observed the phases of Venus: it was one of the proofs that the planets go round the Sun and not round the Earth.
oggetti/terra/cosa: The third planet from the Sun, the one we live on. It's the only known planet with liquid water on its surface and with life. It goes round the Sun in a year, at about 150 million km, and has just one moon: the Moon.
oggetti/terra/quando: Always: you're standing on it. Day and night come from the Earth spinning on itself in 24 hours; the seasons come from its axis being tilted by 23 and a half degrees as it travels round the Sun in a year.
oggetti/terra/dove: Under your feet, third after Mercury and Venus. When you look at the night sky you're always looking away from the Sun: that's why you see different constellations in summer and winter. The Solar System map on this page shows where it is along its orbit today.
oggetti/terra/come: The Earth can be "seen" in the sky in indirect ways. During a lunar eclipse its round shadow covers the Moon: that's how Aristotle already worked out that the Earth is a sphere. In the days around new Moon you can also see earthshine: the dark part of the Moon lit up by light reflected from the Earth. And the slow turning of the whole sky around the Pole Star is really the Earth rotating.
oggetti/terra/origine: The Italian name "Terra" comes from the Latin "terra", from the same root as "torrere" (to dry): "the dry part", as opposed to the sea. It's the only planet not named after a Greek or Roman god, although the Romans worshipped the goddess Tellus, Mother Earth (Gaia to the Greeks).
oggetti/terra/storia: Around 240 BC Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth by comparing the Sun's shadows at Syene and Alexandria, and was only slightly off. In 1543 Copernicus removed it from the centre of the universe and set it going round the Sun. In 1968 the Apollo 8 astronauts photographed the Earth rising above the Moon, and in 1990 the Voyager 1 probe, from 6 billion km away, captured it as a "pale blue dot".
oggetti/marte/cosa: The red planet, covered in dust rich in iron oxide (rust).
oggetti/marte/quando: It's at its brightest and largest at "opposition", which happens about every 26 months.
oggetti/marte/dove: Along the band of the zodiac, the same path the Moon follows.
oggetti/marte/come: To the naked eye you can recognise it by its orange colour. Through a telescope, at the best times, you can glimpse the white polar caps.
oggetti/marte/origine: From the Roman god of war, because of its colour, which recalls blood. The Greeks called it Ares.
oggetti/marte/storia: In 1877 Giovanni Schiaparelli drew "canali" (Italian for "channels") on its surface, a word later wrongly translated into English as "canals", artificial works. Today various rovers are exploring its ground.
oggetti/giove/cosa: The largest planet in the Solar System, a gas giant with more than 90 moons.
oggetti/giove/quando: Visible for many months of the year; it stays in each constellation of the zodiac for about a year.
oggetti/giove/dove: Along the band of the zodiac. It's often the brightest point in the sky after Venus.
oggetti/giove/come: To the naked eye it's a bright, steady point. With binoculars held very still you can see up to four tiny dots beside it: its largest moons.
oggetti/giove/origine: From the king of the Roman gods, Jupiter (Zeus to the Greeks), fitting for the largest planet.
oggetti/giove/storia: In January 1610 Galileo discovered the four largest moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), which he called the "Medicean Planets".
oggetti/saturno/cosa: The ringed planet; the rings are made of ice and rock.
oggetti/saturno/quando: Visible for many months of the year; it moves slowly, staying in one constellation for about two and a half years.
oggetti/saturno/dove: Along the band of the zodiac. It's a pale yellow point.
oggetti/saturno/come: To the naked eye it's a yellowish star. A small telescope at 30-50 times magnification is enough to see the rings.
oggetti/saturno/origine: From the Roman god Saturn, father of Jupiter and god of time and farming: the slowest of the planets visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/saturno/storia: In 1610 Galileo saw two "ears" on either side of the planet. It was Christiaan Huygens, in 1659, who explained that it was a ring.
oggetti/urano/cosa: The seventh planet, a giant of gas and ice four times wider than the Earth. It spins "lying on its side", with its axis almost horizontal.
oggetti/urano/quando: It's best seen from September to February, around opposition (in 2026 at the end of November). You need a dark sky, away from lights and with no Moon.
oggetti/urano/dove: In these years it's in Taurus, between the Pleiades and Aldebaran. It moves very little: it stays in one constellation for about seven years.
oggetti/urano/come: It's at the limit of the naked eye: from a really dark sky it's a very faint little star. With binoculars it's easy, but you need a chart to work out which "star" it is. Through a telescope it becomes a small blue-green disc.
oggetti/urano/origine: From Uranus, the Greek god of the sky, father of Saturn (Cronus) and grandfather of Jupiter: the name continues the family of the gods. Herschel wanted to call it "George's Star" in honour of King George III.
oggetti/urano/storia: The first planet discovered with a telescope: William Herschel found it on 13 March 1781, believing at first that it was a comet. The ancients didn't know it because it's too faint and slow. Only the Voyager 2 probe has visited it, in 1986.
oggetti/nettuno/cosa: The eighth and last planet, a deep blue giant of gas and ice, where the strongest winds in the Solar System blow.
oggetti/nettuno/quando: It's best seen from August to January, around opposition (in 2026 at the end of September). You need a dark sky with no Moon.
oggetti/nettuno/dove: In these years it's in Pisces, not far from Saturn, which helps you find the area. It stays in one constellation for more than ten years.
oggetti/nettuno/come: It's never visible to the naked eye. With good binoculars and a detailed chart it's a dot like lots of other faint stars; with a telescope at high magnification it looks like a tiny blue disc.
oggetti/nettuno/origine: From Neptune, the Roman god of the sea (Poseidon to the Greeks), because of its colour, blue like the ocean.
oggetti/nettuno/storia: The first planet found with mathematics before it was found with eyes. Uranus wasn't following its expected path: the Frenchman Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unknown planet disturbing it had to be, and on 23 September 1846 Johann Galle saw it in Berlin, less than one degree from the predicted spot. Galileo had already seen it in 1612, mistaking it for a star.
oggetti/polare/cosa: A yellow star in Ursa Minor that lies almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole.
oggetti/polare/quando: Always, every night of the year: from Italy it never sets.
oggetti/polare/dove: In the North, at a height equal to your latitude (about 40-45 degrees in Italy). You find it by extending the distance between the two end stars of the Plough 5 times.
oggetti/polare/come: With the naked eye. It isn't the brightest star in the sky, as many people think, but of average brightness.
oggetti/polare/origine: From the Latin "stella polaris", the star of the pole. Its scientific name is Alpha Ursae Minoris.
oggetti/polare/storia: For centuries it guided sailors. It won't be the pole star for ever: because of the precession of the Earth's axis, in about 12,000 years the role will pass to Vega.
oggetti/sirio/cosa: The brightest star in the night sky, 8.6 light years away. It's in Canis Major.
oggetti/sirio/quando: Winter evenings, from December to March.
oggetti/sirio/dove: In the South-East and then in the South. You find it by extending Orion's Belt down and to the left.
oggetti/sirio/come: With the naked eye. When it's low on the horizon it twinkles in every colour because of the atmosphere.
oggetti/sirio/origine: From the Greek "Seirios", "scorching, glowing". The Romans also called it Canicula, "little dog".
oggetti/sirio/storia: The ancient Egyptians waited for its first appearance at dawn, in summer, because it heralded the flooding of the Nile. From Canicula comes the Italian word "canicola" for the summer heatwave, the "dog days" of summer.
oggetti/vega/cosa: A bluish-white star 25 light years away, the brightest in the constellation Lyra.
oggetti/vega/quando: Summer evenings, from June to October, when it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/vega/dove: Very high in the sky in summer. With Altair and Deneb it forms the "Summer Triangle".
oggetti/vega/come: With the naked eye. With binoculars you can see the double star Epsilon Lyrae next to it.
oggetti/vega/origine: From the Arabic "al-nasr al-waqi", "the swooping eagle".
oggetti/vega/storia: It was the first star ever photographed, in 1850. For centuries it was the reference point for the brightness scale (magnitude zero).
oggetti/arturo/cosa: An orange giant 37 light years away, the brightest star in the northern sky. It's in Boötes.
oggetti/arturo/quando: Spring and summer evenings, from April to August.
oggetti/arturo/dove: You find it by following the curve of the Plough's handle: "arc to Arcturus".
oggetti/arturo/come: With the naked eye, easy to recognise by its orange colour.
oggetti/arturo/origine: From the Greek "Arktouros", "guardian of the bear", because it follows the Great Bear on its circuit around the pole.
oggetti/arturo/storia: In 1933 its light, collected by a telescope, switched on the lights of the Chicago World's Fair.
oggetti/betelgeuse/cosa: A red supergiant, Orion's shoulder. If it were in the Sun's place it would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
oggetti/betelgeuse/quando: Winter evenings, from December to March.
oggetti/betelgeuse/dove: Top left in the constellation Orion, looking South.
oggetti/betelgeuse/come: With the naked eye. Comparing it with blue Rigel shows clearly that stars have different colours.
oggetti/betelgeuse/origine: From the Arabic "yad al-jawza", "the hand of al-Jawza" (the Arabic name for Orion). A medieval copying error turned "yad" into "bet".
oggetti/betelgeuse/storia: Between the end of 2019 and the start of 2020 it faded noticeably (the "Great Dimming"). One day it will explode as a supernova.
oggetti/rigel/cosa: A blue supergiant, Orion's foot, thousands of times brighter than the Sun.
oggetti/rigel/quando: Winter evenings, from December to March.
oggetti/rigel/dove: Bottom right in the constellation Orion.
oggetti/rigel/origine: From the Arabic "rijl al-jawza", "the foot of al-Jawza".
oggetti/rigel/storia: Its name appears in the medieval Arabic astronomical tables translated into Latin, which gave us many of the star names we use today.
oggetti/aldebaran/cosa: An orange giant 65 light years away, the eye of Taurus the Bull.
oggetti/aldebaran/dove: By extending Orion's Belt up and to the right. Nearby you can see the V-shaped stars of the Hyades cluster.
oggetti/aldebaran/origine: From the Arabic "al-dabaran", "the follower", because it seems to follow the Pleiades as they move across the sky.
oggetti/aldebaran/storia: The Pioneer 10 probe, launched in 1972, is travelling in its direction: it would reach it in about two million years.
oggetti/antares/cosa: A red supergiant, the heart of Scorpius.
oggetti/antares/quando: Summer evenings, from June to August.
oggetti/antares/dove: Low in the South. From Italy Scorpius never climbs very high above the horizon.
oggetti/antares/come: With the naked eye, red and twinkling.
oggetti/antares/origine: From the Greek "anti-Ares", "rival of Mars", because its red colour is like the planet's.
oggetti/antares/storia: About every two years Mars passes close to it, and the two "rivals" can be compared.
oggetti/altair/cosa: A white star 17 light years away, the brightest in Aquila. It spins so fast that it's flattened.
oggetti/altair/dove: The lowest corner of the "Summer Triangle", with Vega and Deneb.
oggetti/altair/come: With the naked eye. On either side it has two fainter stars that make it easy to recognise.
oggetti/altair/origine: From the Arabic "al-nasr al-tair", "the flying eagle".
oggetti/altair/storia: In a Chinese and Japanese legend (the Tanabata festival) Altair is a herdsman separated from his beloved, Vega, by the Milky Way.
oggetti/deneb/cosa: A white supergiant, the tail of Cygnus. It's one of the most luminous stars in the Galaxy, but very far away (a few thousand light years; the distance is uncertain).
oggetti/deneb/dove: Very high in summer, the third corner of the "Summer Triangle". It sits deep in the Milky Way.
oggetti/deneb/origine: From the Arabic "dhanab al-dajaja", "the hen's tail": that's what the Arabs called Cygnus.
oggetti/deneb/storia: In about 8,000 years it will be the star closest to the north celestial pole.
oggetti/capella/cosa: It's actually four stars, 43 light years away. To the naked eye it looks like a single yellow star, the brightest in Auriga.
oggetti/capella/quando: Autumn and winter evenings. From northern Italy it never sets.
oggetti/capella/dove: High in the North-East in autumn, almost overhead in winter.
oggetti/capella/origine: From the Latin "capella", "little she-goat": in myth it's the goat Amalthea, who suckled the baby Zeus.
oggetti/capella/storia: Near it there's a small triangle of stars called "the Kids".
oggetti/spica/cosa: A blue star (actually a very close pair) about 250 light years away, the brightest in Virgo.
oggetti/spica/quando: Spring evenings, from April to June.
oggetti/spica/dove: By continuing the arc of the Plough beyond Arcturus: "arc to Arcturus, then spike to Spica".
oggetti/spica/origine: From the Latin "spica", "ear of grain": the ear of wheat that Virgo holds in her hand.
oggetti/spica/storia: By comparing Spica's position with older measurements, in the 2nd century BC Hipparchus discovered the precession of the equinoxes.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/cosa: One of the largest constellations. Its seven brightest stars form the Plough.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/quando: All year round: from Italy it never sets. It's highest in spring.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/dove: In the North. In spring it's high, in autumn it's low on the horizon.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/come: With the naked eye. It's the starting point for finding the Pole Star, Arcturus and Spica.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/origine: In Greek myth it's the nymph Callisto, turned into a bear by Hera, Zeus's jealous wife, and then placed in the sky.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/storia: Almost every people of the northern hemisphere has seen something in it: a cart, a plough, seven wise men. Mizar and Alcor, in the handle, were used to test people's eyesight.
oggetti/cassiopea/cosa: Five bright stars in the shape of a W (or an M, depending on the time).
oggetti/cassiopea/quando: All year round: from Italy it never sets. It's highest in autumn.
oggetti/cassiopea/dove: In the North, on the opposite side of the Pole Star from the Plough.
oggetti/cassiopea/come: With the naked eye. With binoculars, in the area between Cassiopeia and Perseus, you can see the Double Cluster.
oggetti/cassiopea/origine: The queen of Ethiopia in myth, mother of Andromeda, punished by Poseidon for her vanity and condemned to circle the pole, sometimes upside down.
oggetti/cassiopea/storia: In 1572 Tycho Brahe observed a "new star" there (a supernova), which proved that even the sky of the stars changes.
oggetti/orione/cosa: The most famous constellation of the winter sky: a hunter with shoulders, a belt of three stars and feet.
oggetti/orione/dove: In the South. The three stars in a row of the Belt (Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka) are the easiest landmark.
oggetti/orione/come: With the naked eye. Below the Belt, in the "sword", lies the Orion Nebula, which you can see with binoculars too.
oggetti/orione/origine: The giant hunter of Greek myth, killed by a scorpion. That's why Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky together.
oggetti/orione/storia: It already appears in the Iliad and the Odyssey. The ancient Egyptians linked it to the god Osiris.
oggetti/scorpione/cosa: A zodiac constellation shaped like a scorpion, with its tail curled up.
oggetti/scorpione/quando: Summer evenings, from June to August.
oggetti/scorpione/dove: Low in the South. From southern Italy you can see the whole tail, from the north only part of it.
oggetti/scorpione/come: With the naked eye, from a dark place with a clear southern horizon.
oggetti/scorpione/origine: The scorpion sent to kill Orion. The gods placed them on opposite sides of the sky, so they would never meet again.
oggetti/scorpione/storia: The ancient Romans also included the stars of Libra in it, which they called "the claws".
oggetti/cigno/cosa: A swan in flight with its wings spread along the Milky Way; its shape is also called the "Northern Cross".
oggetti/cigno/dove: High in the sky in summer. Deneb is the tail, Albireo the beak.
oggetti/cigno/come: With the naked eye. With a small telescope, Albireo shows up as a pair of stars, one yellow and one blue.
oggetti/cigno/origine: In myth, Zeus turned himself into a swan to get close to Leda, queen of Sparta.
oggetti/cigno/storia: Cygnus contains Cygnus X-1, the first object recognised as a black hole, in the early 1970s.
oggetti/leone/cosa: One of the few constellations that really looks like its figure: a crouching lion. The head is a back-to-front "question mark".
oggetti/leone/quando: Spring evenings, from March to May.
oggetti/leone/dove: In the South in spring. The brightest star is Regulus, at the bottom of the question mark.
oggetti/leone/origine: The Nemean lion killed by Hercules in the first of his twelve labours. Regulus comes from the Latin "regulus", "little king".
oggetti/leone/storia: Every year in mid-November the Leonid shooting stars seem to come from Leo; in 1833 and 1966 they produced real meteor "storms".
oggetti/pleiadi/cosa: A cluster of young stars about 440 light years away, in Taurus.
oggetti/pleiadi/dove: By extending Orion's Belt beyond Aldebaran. They look like a small cloud of stars.
oggetti/pleiadi/come: With the naked eye you can count 6 or 7. Binoculars are the ideal instrument: you can see dozens.
oggetti/pleiadi/origine: In myth they are the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. In English they're also called the "Seven Sisters"; in Italian they have the nicknames "Sette Sorelle" (Seven Sisters) and "Gallinelle" (Little Hens).
oggetti/pleiadi/storia: They may appear on the Nebra Sky Disc, about 3,600 years old. In Japan they're called Subaru, like the car brand that has them in its logo.
oggetti/andromeda/cosa: The nearest large galaxy to our own, with hundreds of billions of stars, 2.5 million light years away. It's the most distant object visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/andromeda/quando: Evenings from August to February; best in autumn.
oggetti/andromeda/dove: High in autumn. You find it starting from Cassiopeia or from the Square of Pegasus.
oggetti/andromeda/come: From a dark sky, far from towns, you can see it with the naked eye as a small elongated smudge. With binoculars it becomes a glowing spindle.
oggetti/andromeda/origine: From the constellation it lies in: Andromeda, the princess of myth rescued by Perseus.
oggetti/andromeda/storia: The Persian astronomer al-Sufi described it in 964 as a "little cloud". Only in 1923-24 did Edwin Hubble prove that it's another galaxy.
oggetti/nebulosa-orione/cosa: A great cloud of gas where new stars are being born, about 1,350 light years away.
oggetti/nebulosa-orione/dove: In Orion's "sword", below the three stars of the Belt.
oggetti/nebulosa-orione/come: To the naked eye it looks like a blurry star. With binoculars you can see the faint mist; with a telescope the Trapezium appears, four stars in the middle.
oggetti/nebulosa-orione/origine: It takes its name from the constellation. M42 is its number in Charles Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/nebulosa-orione/storia: It was first described in 1610 by Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc. It's one of the most photographed nebulae.
oggetti/presepe/cosa: A cluster of stars about 600 light years away, in Cancer.
oggetti/presepe/dove: Halfway between Gemini and Regulus in Leo, in the faint constellation Cancer.
oggetti/presepe/come: To the naked eye, from a dark sky, it's a hazy patch. Binoculars resolve it into lots of stars.
oggetti/presepe/origine: Its Latin name is "Praesepe", "manger" (in Italian "Presepe"); in English it's usually called the Beehive. The two nearby stars are called the Aselli, the little donkeys eating from the manger.
oggetti/presepe/storia: In 1609-10 Galileo pointed his spyglass at it and counted more than 40 stars where before only a cloud could be seen.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/cosa: Two star clusters close together, about 7,500 light years away.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/quando: Evenings from September to March. From northern Italy it never sets.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/dove: Between Cassiopeia and Perseus, in the North-East in autumn.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/come: From a dark sky, with the naked eye, it's a small smudge. With binoculars two groups of stars appear side by side: a wonderful sight.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/origine: The name describes its shape. The catalogue calls them NGC 869 and NGC 884, or h and Chi Persei.
oggetti/doppio-ammasso/storia: It was already known to the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, in the 2nd century BC.
oggetti/m13/cosa: A globular cluster: a ball of hundreds of thousands of very old stars, about 22,000 light years away.
oggetti/m13/dove: In the constellation Hercules, between Vega and Arcturus, on one side of the four-sided shape called the "Keystone".
oggetti/m13/come: With binoculars it's a fuzzy little ball. With a medium telescope you start to see individual stars at the edges.
oggetti/m13/origine: From the constellation Hercules, the hero of the twelve labours.
oggetti/m13/storia: Discovered by Edmond Halley in 1714. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope sent it a radio message, which will arrive in about 22,000 years.
